When the real-life Dolores Fuller first read the screenplay for Ed Wood, she was deeply offended by her portrayal, feeling the script unfairly reduced her to a one-dimensional, nagging shrew while ignoring the genuine financial and emotional support she provided to Wood early in his career. To rectify this, Sarah Jessica Parker deliberately approached the role not as a primary antagonist, but as the only grounded voice of reason trapped in an increasingly surreal and unsustainable environment. Parker infused the character with a sympathetic, palpable exhaustion, focusing on the agonizing reality of loving a relentlessly optimistic, angora-obsessed filmmaker who continually drained their finances to fund cinematic disasters. This nuanced, humanizing performance completely changed Fuller’s mind; upon seeing the finished film, she publicly praised Parker for accurately capturing the unique frustration of her time with the eccentric director.

Ed Wood (1994), directed by Tim Burton, starring Johnny Depp, Martin Landau, Sarah Jessica Parker, Patricia Arquette. An ambitious but hopelessly untalented film director relies on his unwavering optimism, an eclectic troupe of Hollywood misfits, and the aging horror star Bela Lugosi to create a series of spectacularly terrible low-budget movies in 1950s Los Angeles.
